Agentic AI in AML: where agents fit in alert work

MT

Mehak Tariq, CAMSNovember 25, 2026•8 min read

Agentic AI in AML means using AI agents to carry out multi-step compliance work. Given an alert, an agent plans the steps, calls the systems that hold the transactions, the customer profile and past alerts, applies the team's written rules and drafts a note for an analyst. The decisions that carry legal weight, such as closing an alert, escalating a case or filing a suspicious activity report (SAR), stay with named people on the compliance team.

This guide covers the bank side: the written procedure, an L1 alert run, the stop points, the log and the testing. It explains public guidance and is not legal advice.

What agentic AI means for AML teams

A monitoring system raises alerts and a screening tool compares names with lists. An agent works across those tools: given a task such as "triage this alert", it decides which data to fetch, fetches it, checks it against the procedure and produces an output a person can review.

US agencies have encouraged innovative approaches, including artificial intelligence, since the 2018 joint statement on innovative efforts to combat money laundering, in which the Federal Reserve, FDIC, FinCEN, NCUA and OCC said they "will not advocate a particular method or technology". The new interagency model risk guidance leaves agents out. Footnote 3 of the interagency guidance issued as SR 26-2 in April 2026 says generative and agentic AI models "are not within the scope of this guidance", leaving each bank's own risk management and governance practices to set the controls. For now, the procedure, stop points and run log are the practical way to show those controls. See what SR 26-2 changes for banks.

Where AI agents for AML compliance fit

The FFIEC BSA/AML Examination Manual breaks suspicious activity monitoring into five components. Agents fit some far better than others:

FFIEC componentWhat an agent can doWhat stays with people
Identification or alert of unusual activityLittle: alerts still come from monitoring systems and referralsOwning and tuning rules and thresholds
Managing alertsGather context, apply the disposition rules, draft the rationaleConfirming each closure and escalation
SAR decision makingAssemble the case fileThe filing decision
SAR completion and filingCollect the supporting documents the procedure namesWriting, approving and filing the SAR
Continuing activityPull activity since the last reviewDeciding whether to file again

The same pattern carries into level 2 work and AML investigations: the agent assembles the timeline, counterparties and documents, and the investigator draws the conclusion.

Start with the written procedure

The FFIEC manual says policies and procedures "should describe the steps the bank takes to address each component and indicate the person(s) or departments responsible", with "a clear and defined escalation process from the point of initial detection to disposition of the investigation." An agent needs that document written precisely enough to run. For each step it should state:

  • which systems and fields the step reads, and over what look-back period;
  • the rule, as a testable condition for recommending closure or routing to an analyst;
  • where a named role must decide before anything happens;
  • what the output must contain, in the team's case note template;
  • which version is in force and who approved it.

How AI agents for transaction monitoring run an L1 alert

Take an alert on a business account where wires from a new counterparty exceed expected activity. The table shows one way to run it; your steps, look-back period and thresholds come from your own risk assessment.

StepWhat the agent doesStops for an analyst whenWhat is logged
1. IntakeReads the alert, the rule that fired, the score and the accountAlert data is missingAlert ID, time received, procedure version
2. Gather contextPulls transactions, the customer profile, expected activity and earlier alertsA source system does not respondEach source queried and what came back
3. Screen counterpartiesScreens counterparties named in the alertAny possible matchThe screening result
4. Apply the rulesCompares activity with the expected profile using the disposition rulesScore above the review threshold, or activity the profile does not explainEach rule, its inputs and result
5. Draft the noteWrites the rationale in the team's template, citing its dataA statement has no sourceThe draft and its citations
6. Analyst decisionHands over the alert with context assembledAlwaysReviewer, decision, reason, time
7. EscalationOpens the level 2 case and attaches the fileThe investigator takes overCase reference, handoff time

Using an agent does not change when the SAR clock starts. Under 31 CFR 1020.320, a bank must file no later than 30 calendar days after initial detection of facts that may constitute a basis for a SAR, with up to 30 more days to identify a suspect and no more than 60 in total. The FFIEC manual adds that "initial detection" should not be read as "the moment a transaction is highlighted for review"; the period starts when a review determines the activity is suspicious. Log when the reviewer, at level 1 or level 2, determined the activity suspicious. See the alert triage use case for this run with sample data.

Where the agent must stop

These decisions should pause the run until a named person decides:

  • Closing an alert. The agent recommends; an analyst confirms.
  • Any possible sanctions screening match.
  • Escalation and the SAR decision. The FFIEC manual says the decision maker "should have the authority to make the final SAR filing decision."
  • Customer exits and changes to the level of due diligence.
  • Anything the procedure does not cover, such as missing data or conflicting records.

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework calls for policies that "define and differentiate roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations and oversight of AI systems." The FATF's 2021 report on new technologies says "manual review and human input remains very important". In the EU, Article 76(5) of the Anti-Money Laundering Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, which applies from July 10, 2027, allows decisions from automated processes and AI systems only on conditions. One is that decisions to enter, refuse or maintain a business relationship, or to change the level of due diligence, be "subject to meaningful human intervention".

What to log on every run

The log shows an examiner that the agent followed the procedure and people made the decisions. For each alert, keep:

  • the procedure version and agent configuration in force;
  • each data source queried and what came back;
  • each rule checked, with inputs and result;
  • the draft note and the data it cites;
  • each pause: who it went to, why and when;
  • the analyst's decision, reason and time, and whether it differed from the agent's recommendation.

NIST notes that data on "the frequency and rationale with which humans overrule AI system output" may be useful to collect and analyze.

Record rules still apply around the log. The October 2025 interagency SAR FAQs say there is no "requirement or expectation" to document a decision not to file, and that, where a team chooses to document one, "In most cases, a short, concise statement documenting a financial institution's SAR decision will likely suffice". When a SAR is filed, 31 CFR 1020.320(d) requires keeping a copy and the supporting documentation "for a period of five years from the date of filing the SAR." SARs are also confidential under the same section, so limit who can read logs that touch SAR decisions. In the EU, Article 77 of the AMLR requires a record of the assessment carried out under Article 69(2), "whether or not such assessment results in a suspicious transaction report being made to the FIU".

Test it before it goes live

  1. Build an evaluation set from alerts the team has already worked: closures, escalations, screening hits, missing data. The expected result is the documented human decision.
  2. Run the agent against that set in a sandbox, then in parallel with the existing process, and compare its recommendations, stop points and notes with what your analysts did.
  3. Track agreement with analysts, escalations the agent would have missed (the number that matters most), how often it routes to a person and how often analysts overrule it.
  4. Test again whenever the procedure, the model, a data source or a threshold changes.

The 2018 joint statement says pilot programs run alongside existing BSA/AML processes "in and of themselves should not subject banks to supervisory criticism even if the pilot programs ultimately prove unsuccessful." It leaves bank management to judge when an approach is ready to replace or augment existing processes, and to discuss that with its regulators. NIST asks for performance "demonstrated for conditions similar to deployment setting(s)", so test on your own alerts.

What examiners and model risk guidance expect

Examiners work from the FFIEC manual, which expects this of monitoring systems: management "should document and be able to explain filtering criteria, thresholds used, and how both are appropriate for the bank's risks", and the system's methodology and effectiveness should be independently validated. The agent sits outside SR 26-2, but a machine-learning score that ranks its alerts is a non-generative, non-agentic AI model, which the guidance covers. Keep both in your inventory, and put the vendor and its model provider through third-party risk management, a factor the 2018 statement names.

How to evaluate agentic AI software for AML

When you compare agentic AI AML solutions, ask:

  • Does it run from your written procedure, and does each run record the version it followed?
  • Can your team set the stop points as conditions it can read and test?
  • Can it be kept from closing alerts, filing reports or contacting customers?
  • Can an examiner follow the run log without the vendor in the room, and can the log be altered?
  • Can you test a new version against your own past alerts in a sandbox first?
  • Which data leaves your environment, and which model provider processes it?

As one example, Verkflo compiles a written procedure into a versioned spec, tests it with evals and a sandbox before live mode, pauses for review where your rules say, and records each run in a hash-chained audit log; see AML automation and sanctions screening use case.

Common questions

How can AI be used in AML?

AI is used for scoring in monitoring systems, name matching in screening, and, more recently, agents that gather context and draft notes for alert triage, screening hits, PEP and adverse media reviews and KYC reviews.

How is AI being used to improve AML compliance?

The aim is to cut the time analysts spend collecting data before they can judge an alert, and to apply the written procedure the same way on every review.

Will AML jobs be replaced by AI?

The guidance does not point that way. The FFIEC expects a decision maker with authority over SAR filings, and the EU AMLR requires meaningful human intervention in key customer decisions. On that guidance, the work is more likely to shift toward reviewing, deciding and investigating.

Can an AI agent decide whether to file a SAR?

It should not. The FFIEC manual gives the final filing decision to an individual or committee with the authority to make it. An agent can assemble the file they read.
